# Commutation of the groups generated by orthogonal simple roots

Authors: Worker 1490 and Worker 1444.

The theorem `Langlands.GroupScheme.orthogonalSimpleRootCommutation.{u}`
proves `Langlands.GroupScheme.OrthogonalSimpleRootCommutationStatement.{u}`.
It imports the [published statement](OrthogonalSimpleRootCommutationStatement.md)
unchanged.

For every field `k : Type u`, actual affine group scheme `G` over `Spec k`
and supplied split pinning `p`,
let `a` and `b` be distinct orthogonal simple roots in the pinning's base.
On every scheme test `Z`, all elements of

```
U(a)(Z) ⊔ U(-a)(Z)
```

commute with all elements of

```
U(b)(Z) ⊔ U(-b)(Z).
```

Here `U(c)` is the intrinsic subgroup functor
`RelativeRoot.subgroup p.inclusion c`, and each supremum is taken in the group
of actual morphisms `Z ⟶ G.X`. The conclusion includes nonreduced tests.
The split pinning is supplied data, not an existence conclusion. The field
may be finite or imperfect, and the universe remains arbitrary.

## Implemented proof

The proof first excludes every strict positive combination of a signed root
from each of the two simple-root pairs.

`SplitPinning.strict_mixed_simple_ne_zero_not_root` uses the linear
independence of the base and
`LeviGluing.mixed_not_mem_positiveClosure`. For positive natural numbers
`n` and `m`, neither `n a - m b` nor its negative lies in the nonnegative
additive monoid generated by the simple roots. Zero lies in that monoid,
so the combination is nonzero. Every root or its negative lies in the
monoid by the base's sign property. The combination therefore cannot be
an actual root. The proof uses `p.isRootDatum` to identify the supplied
root datum's root range with the roots of the actual torus inclusion.

`SplitPinning.strict_positive_orthogonal_simple_ne_zero_not_root`
reflects `n a + m b` in `a`. Orthogonality makes the result `m b - n a`,
which the preceding lemma excludes. Reflection preserves zero and the
root range, proving the exclusion for the positive combination.

`SplitPinning.strict_signed_orthogonal_simple_ne_zero_not_root` treats the
four possible choices of signs. The mixed cases use the first lemma,
interchanging the two simple roots when necessary. The negative-negative
case uses the positive case and closure of the root range under negation.
Thus every `n c + m d`, where `c` is either sign of `a`, `d` is either
sign of `b`, and both coefficients are positive, is nonzero and is not a root.

`SplitPinning.commute_of_no_strict_root_combinations` converts this root
exclusion into commutation. For nonzero characters `c` and `d`, the
published equality `RelativeRoot.weightFiltration_one_eq_subgroup`
identifies each intrinsic root subgroup with its generated first cyclic
tail under conjugation. The literal sum of those cyclic tails consists of
the strict combinations just considered. Every such character is nonzero,
so `RelativeRoot.mem_actionWeightSupport_conjugation_iff` identifies
occurrence as an ambient conjugation weight with being a root. The
root exclusions make this semigroup have no ambient occurring weights.
Consequently
`RelativeRoot.semigroupSubgroup_eq_bot_of_noAmbientWeights_without_realization`
makes its generated subgroup the identity subgroup.

The unconditional theorem `RelativeRoot.semigroupCommutator` places the
commutator of the two root-subgroup elements in that identity subgroup.
The commutator identity gives `Commute x y`. Smoothness, required by the
cyclic-tail comparison and commutator theorem, comes from
`p.isConnectedReductive.smooth`; no additional hypothesis is introduced.
`SplitPinning.commute_signed_orthogonal_simple` supplies nonzeroness of the
signed characters from the root datum and applies this argument to all
four sign choices.

Finally, the closing theorem applies elementary subgroup centralizers.
Each of the four generator subgroups centralizes the appropriate subgroup
from the other pair. The symmetry
`Subgroup.le_centralizer_iff` and the universal property of subgroup
suprema extend these containments to both generated groups. Evaluating
the resulting containment at the supplied elements proves the exact
statement.

## Provenance and application boundary

This is an internal deduction from the published intrinsic-root,
semigroup-commutator and weight-triviality theorems, together with
Mathlib's root-pairing and subgroup-centralizer APIs.
`Reductive.SplitLeviGluingMixedRoots` supplies the positive-monoid exclusion
and the model for the commutator argument; its existing commutation theorem
uses simple roots defined by a generic cocharacter, whereas this proof
works directly with the base of the supplied split pinning.

The motivating argument is R. Steinberg, *Regular elements of semi-simple
algebraic groups* (1965), Theorem 9.4 and its proof, printed pp.72–73 /
PDF pp.25–26: representatives chosen in the corresponding rank-one groups
commute within an orthogonal orbit of simple roots. The root-subgroup
background is in Sections 2.1–2.2, printed p.52 / PDF p.5. Registered
source `steinberg-1965-regular-elements-semisimple-groups`, SHA-256
`bda20c4a4b3cf4a7e9e5b17a4eacd0147d0c9370063ab3a3778114a53c8349b9`.
Steinberg's Section 9 assumes a perfect ground field and a simply connected
semisimple group, inside an algebraically closed universal field.
The implemented proof uses the published scheme-theoretic weight bounds
to obtain commutation on all tests over every field for the supplied split
pinning. This broader all-test assertion is a derived deduction, rather than
a literal transcription of Theorem 9.4.

The proof was developed by Worker 1490 in the parent Steinberg-quotient draft.
Worker 1444 prepared this focused submission against the published statement
and checked the proof and source comparison.

The theorem constructs neither root parametrizations nor root-generated
reflection representatives. It does not assert commutation for arbitrary
reflection representatives with torus factors, or for arbitrary orthogonal
roots that are not simple in the same base. The existence and Galois
compatibility of representatives, descent of a cross-section, and its
comparison with the canonical quotient remain separate obligations.
